question: PE ratios of 10 companies: 12,14,15,16,18,19,20,22,25,120. Which central tendency measure for comparable set?
before: Median. PE 120 is massive outlier pulling mean to ~28.1 (describes none). Median = (18+19)/2 = 18.5 -- far more representative. Mode not applicable (no repeats). Geometric mean not used for cross-sectional PE.
after:
Concept: Central tendency measures describe the typical value in a dataset. The median is the middle value when data are ordered; the mean is the arithmetic average; the mode is the most frequent value; the geometric mean is the nth root of the product of n values.

Step-by-step: Order the 10 PE ratios: 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 19, 20, 22, 25, 120. With n=10 (even), the median is the average of the 5th and 6th values: (18 + 19) / 2 = 18.5. The mean, by contrast, is (12 + 14 + 15 + 16 + 18 + 19 + 20 + 22 + 25 + 120) / 10 = 281 / 10 = 28.1.

Result: Median = 18.5; Mean = 28.1

Why this is correct: The PE ratio of 120 is an extreme outlier that pulls the mean to 28.1, which misrepresents the typical valuation of the 9 companies clustered between 12 and 25. The median of 18.5 remains unaffected by extreme values and is far more representative of the comparable set.

Why the others are wrong: A) Mean is distorted by the outlier value of 120 and yields 28.1, which does not reflect the central tendency of the majority of companies. C) Mode does not apply here because no PE ratio repeats in the dataset. D) Geometric mean is designed for growth rates, returns, or ratios over time, not for cross-sectional valuation multiples where arithmetic relationships matter more.

Intuition: In equity research, when building comparable company valuations, you must filter or downweight outliers rather than let them dominate. The median is the robust choice for a peer set with one extreme value, ensuring your valuation benchmark reflects the typical peer rather than a distortion.
